Query: How does Button handle deep linking?
Response:
Button handles deep linking as part of a broader mobile routing and conversion optimization layer, not just as a static “open this app URL” tool.

Here’s the practical flow:

A user taps a commerce link
This could come from an affiliate, creator, publisher app, social platform, mobile web page, or offer placement.

Button evaluates the best destination in real time
Button says its Dynamic Decisioning analyzes signals like whether the retailer app is installed and what path is most likely to convert. It can then choose between opening the app, prompting an install, deep linking, or routing to mobile web. 
Button

Button routes to the optimal brand property
In Button’s publisher SDK setup, the publisher passes Button a destination brand URL. Button’s SDK then creates a “Purchase Path” to handle optimized deep linking, attribution, and cross-app user experience. 
Button Developers

If the app is installed, Button can deep link into it
The goal is to take the user directly into the retailer’s app experience instead of dumping them on a generic mobile web page.

If the app is not installed, Button can support install flows or fallback
Button references “Attended Install Technology” for driving app installs, and also offers a Button Browser mobile web view fallback when the brand lacks an app or the user does not want to install it. 
Button Developers

Attribution remains connected
Button positions itself as a bridge between affiliate/creator traffic, mobile measurement partners, and retailer apps, with deterministic data connecting a tap to an app install and purchase where available. 
Button

In simpler terms: Button takes a normal commerce or affiliate link and turns it into a smart mobile route. It decides whether the user should go to the retailer app, app store/install path, in-app product page, or mobile web fallback, while preserving tracking and attribution.

Query: What is Button and should my company use Button?
Response:
Button is a mobile commerce optimization platform. In plain English: it helps retailers, publishers, creators, and affiliate programs make shopping links work better on mobile—especially when a shopper taps from TikTok, Instagram, a publisher article, email, or an affiliate link.

Button’s core value is routing each tap to the highest-converting destination: opening the retailer’s app, sending the user to mobile web, prompting an app install, or deep-linking to a relevant product/page. Button says its Dynamic Decisioning product uses AI to choose that post-click path in real time and improve conversion, attribution, and app revenue. 
Button

What Button does

Button appears to focus on four connected use cases:

Use case	What it means
Mobile deep linking	Sends users from a link directly into an app or relevant mobile destination instead of a generic landing page.
Affiliate / creator commerce optimization	Improves conversion and tracking from affiliate, creator, and publisher traffic.
App acquisition and app revenue	Turns affiliate/social traffic into app installs and in-app purchases.
Retail media / shoppable content	Helps publishers and retailers create commerce experiences and monetize product-focused content.

Button says it has driven $100B+ in sales, 22M app installs, and optimized 5,000+ apps, according to its own website. 
Button
 It also promotes a Full Service Network for launching and optimizing affiliate programs across retailers and publishers. 
Button

Should your company use Button?

Yes, Button is worth evaluating if your company has meaningful mobile commerce traffic and cares about affiliate, creator, publisher, or app-driven revenue.

It is most relevant if you are:

A retailer or marketplace with a mobile app
Button is strongest when there is value in pushing shoppers into the app, improving app installs, and tracking in-app purchases from affiliate/creator traffic.

Running affiliate or creator programs
Button positions itself as a way to fix mobile affiliate journeys where standard links lose attribution, send users to poor mobile web experiences, or fail to detect whether the app is installed. 
Button

A publisher, creator network, or commerce content business
Button’s marketplace and CuratedBy products are aimed at monetizing shoppable content and improving revenue from product links. 
Button

Already using affiliate networks but struggling with app attribution
Button’s Reach product is described as deep-linking and app-tracking technology for affiliate network traffic; Awin was cited as an early network integration. 
Button

When Button probably makes sense

Button likely deserves a serious look if you can answer “yes” to several of these:

Question	Why it matters
Do we have a consumer mobile app?	Button’s biggest value is routing users into app journeys.
Do app shoppers convert better than mobile web shoppers?	The ROI depends on app conversion / LTV upside.
Do we get traffic from affiliates, influencers, publishers, or social commerce?	Button optimizes exactly those post-click paths.
Are we losing attribution when users move from link → app → purchase?	Button emphasizes deterministic tracking and network/MMP connectivity.
Do we want more app installs from non-Google/non-Meta channels?	Button claims affiliate traffic can become an app acquisition channel.
When Button may not be a fit

I would be cautious if:

Situation	Why
You do not have a mobile app	Button’s app-routing value is reduced.
Your ecommerce volume is low	Enterprise-oriented optimization may not justify the integration and platform cost.
Most traffic is desktop or logged-in web	The mobile deep-linking problem is less acute.
You do not use affiliates, creators, publishers, or social commerce	Button’s core channel advantage may not apply.
You already have best-in-class deep linking, MMP attribution, and affiliate app tracking	Button may be incremental rather than transformational.
Evidence to ask Button for

Button publishes strong performance claims, including a 2026 commissioned Forrester TEI study reporting 432% ROI, $3.4M NPV over three years, and payback in under six months for a composite $1B B2C retailer. Because that study was commissioned by Button, treat it as useful directional evidence, not a guaranteed outcome. 
Button
+1

A good diligence process would ask Button for:

Area	What to request
Baseline audit	Current mobile web vs app conversion, EPC, install rate, and attribution gaps.
Incrementality	A holdout or A/B test plan, not just before/after reporting.
Network compatibility	Confirm support for your affiliate networks, MMP, analytics, and privacy setup.
Commercial model	Fees, commission impact, implementation cost, and required contract length.
Data governance	How Button handles user-level data, consent, privacy opt-outs, and attribution limitations.
Practical recommendation

Use Button if your company is a mobile-first retailer, marketplace, publisher, or creator-commerce business with real affiliate/social traffic and a valuable app. In that case, Button could improve revenue by reducing mobile friction, increasing app opens/installs, and improving attribution.

Do not prioritize Button if your business is mostly desktop, does not have an app, or does not rely on affiliate/creator/publisher commerce. In that case, your resources may be better spent on site conversion, lifecycle marketing, SEO, paid acquisition, or a lighter-weight deep-linking solution.

My recommendation: evaluate Button with a controlled pilot focused on one measurable KPI—for example mobile affiliate revenue, app install rate from affiliate traffic, in-app conversion rate, or mobile EPC. Do not buy it purely as “AI optimization”; buy it only if Button can prove incremental lift on your actual traffic.

Query: What are the pros and cons of using Button?
Response:
Button is strongest when the problem is mobile affiliate, creator, or publisher traffic that is not converting cleanly because of broken deep links, poor app routing, or attribution gaps. It is less compelling if you mainly need a broad ecommerce suite, merchandising tool, A/B testing platform, personalization engine, or checkout optimization product.

Pros

1. Strong fit for mobile commerce and app-first brands
Button is built around improving post-click shopping journeys through identity, deep linking, machine learning, and mobile routing. Its public positioning is specifically around improving mobile marketing, ad performance, affiliate, creator, and social traffic—not general ecommerce operations. 
Button
+1

2. Can improve affiliate and creator monetization
Button says its platform addresses revenue loss from broken experiences, inconsistent mobile deep linking, and faulty attribution. It also claims its commerce optimization product has driven 20%+ EPC lift on mobile web and 100%+ improvement on social traffic for creator network and publisher partners. Treat those as vendor-reported figures, but they point to the core value prop. 
Button

3. Works alongside existing affiliate ecosystems
Button appears designed as an optimization layer rather than a full replacement for affiliate networks. Acceleration Partners says Button’s PostTap integrates with major networks such as Awin, Impact, Partnerize, CJ, and Rakuten, while impact.com describes Button’s integration as helping with mobile traffic routing, app sales tracking, and partner management. 
Acceleration Partners
+1

4. Useful when app conversion outperforms mobile web
The case for Button gets stronger when your app converts materially better than mobile web. impact.com cites Button-related results including average app conversion rates 200% higher than mobile web in 2023, and Acceleration Partners cites Button’s claim that app shoppers convert 3x higher on average than web shoppers. 
impact.com
+1

5. Public case studies suggest meaningful upside
Button’s case-study page lists examples including Sam’s Club reporting a 165% increase in total mobile affiliate revenue, Awin and Button more than doubling in-app conversion rates, impact.com seeing apps drive 200% the revenue of web journeys, CJ increasing influencer conversion rates by over 400%, Wowcher increasing ROAS by 232%, and Uber doubling affiliate revenue. These are vendor-published case studies, so they should be validated in diligence. 
Button

Cons

1. Narrower than “ecommerce optimization” may imply
Button is not a full ecommerce platform like Shopify, BigCommerce, or WooCommerce, and it is not primarily a site-search, pricing, CRO, merchandising, loyalty, or checkout platform. Its sweet spot is mobile post-click routing and affiliate/creator/publisher traffic optimization.

2. ROI depends on your traffic mix
Button is most likely to matter if you have meaningful mobile, social, affiliate, creator, or publisher-driven commerce traffic. If most revenue comes from desktop, owned CRM, paid search to web checkout, marketplace sales, or low-app-intent users, the upside may be limited.

3. Requires integration and operational coordination
Even if Button describes some publisher solutions as low-code, real value likely depends on link behavior, app configuration, affiliate network setup, tracking, attribution rules, reporting, and partner workflows. That means product, marketing, analytics, mobile engineering, and affiliate teams may all need to be involved.

4. Vendor-reported performance claims need validation
Many of the strongest performance numbers are from Button, partner blogs, or case studies. They are useful directional evidence, but not the same as an independent benchmark. You would want a pilot with holdouts, clean incrementality measurement, and pre-agreed success metrics.

5. Potential overlap with existing tools
If your affiliate network, MMP, deep-linking provider, attribution stack, or app-linking infrastructure already handles routing and in-app attribution well, Button may duplicate functionality. The key question is whether Button improves revenue beyond what Branch, AppsFlyer, Adjust, your affiliate network, and your internal link handling already provide.

Best-fit use cases

Button is worth serious consideration if you have an app, significant affiliate or creator traffic, a meaningful mobile conversion gap, and evidence that users convert better in-app than on mobile web. It is especially relevant for retailers, travel, marketplaces, delivery, rideshare, and other app-based commerce brands.

Poor-fit use cases

Button is probably not the first tool to evaluate if you need general ecommerce infrastructure, website personalization, catalog management, landing page testing, pricing optimization, Shopify app replacement, or broad merchandising analytics.

Bottom line

Use Button if your main issue is turning mobile affiliate/creator/social clicks into higher-converting app or mobile journeys with better attribution. Do not use it as a general ecommerce optimization platform unless that specific mobile post-click problem is one of your biggest revenue leaks.
